Timeline::minute_scalar¶

Back to Timeline API Reference

Signature¶

int Timeline::minute_scalar() const

Read One Minute Within The Hour¶

minute_scalar() extracts the local clock’s minute field, 0..59, from one rank-zero Timeline. It is a component, not a duration: 30 means the instant is thirty minutes into its displayed hour, not that it is thirty minutes from another instant.

The method is useful where a single C++ integer is the desired result. Its array counterpart, minute(), returns a shape-preserving Series. No implicit squeeze occurs, so shape [1] remains non-scalar and is rejected.

Example: Clock Components Remain Separate¶

const auto t = pluss::timeline::make("2025-01-01T01:30:45Z");
std::cout << "hour=" << t.hour_scalar()
          << ", minute=" << t.minute_scalar()
          << ", second=" << t.second_scalar() << '\n';

Output¶

hour=1, minute=30, second=45

Example: Timezone Conversion¶

const auto utc = pluss::timeline::make("2025-01-01T01:30:45Z");
const auto local = utc.tz_convert("America/Edmonton");
std::cout << "UTC=" << utc.minute_scalar()
          << ", Edmonton=" << local.minute_scalar() << '\n';

Output¶

UTC=30, Edmonton=30

Here the offset is an exact number of hours, so the minute happens to remain unchanged. That is a result of this zone and instant, not a promise of timezone conversion; zones with sub-hour offsets can change the minute field.

Example: Absent Instant¶

std::cout << pluss::timeline::make("").minute_scalar() << '\n';

Output¶

-1

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Valid output is 0..59; -1 denotes NaT.

  • Rank-one and higher Timelines throw, even with one element.

  • The method reads local civil time and does not round the instant.

  • Nanoseconds below the second remain intact in the receiver.

See Also¶

  • minute(): shape-preserving extraction.

  • minutes_between(): elapsed whole-minute distance.

  • set_minute(): replace the local minute field.
